author: Gieve Patel
poem_text_en:
It takes much time to kill a tree,
Not a simple jab of the knife
Will do it. It has grown
Slowly consuming the earth,
Rising out of it, feeding
Upon its crust, absorbing
Years of sunlight, air, water,
And out of its leperous hide
Sprouting leaves.

So hack and chop
But this alone wont do it.
Not so much pain will do it.
The bleeding bark will heal
And from close to the ground
Will rise curled green twigs,
Miniature boughs
Which if unchecked will expand again
To former size.

No,
The root is to be pulled out – 
Out of the anchoring earth;
It is to be roped, tied,
And pulled out – snapped out
Or pulled out entirely,
Out from the earth-cave,
And the strength of the tree exposed
The source, white and wet,
The most sensitive, hidden
For years inside the earth.

Then the matter
Of scorching and choking
In sun and air,
Browning, hardening,
Twisting, withering,
And then it is done.
summary_en: The poem illustrates the resilience of a tree and explains that a simple physical attack like hacking or chopping cannot destroy it. It argues that to truly kill a tree, one must extract its roots from the earth, effectively exposing its core to the elements until it withers and dies. The poem serves as a critique of human cruelty toward nature and highlights the enduring strength of the natural world.

glossary.meaning_en: to poke, or thrust abruptly or sharply with a short, quick blow
the brown, hard outer portion or surface

figures_of_speech.note_en: The sap flowing from a cut is compared to blood.
The rough, discolored bark of the tree is compared to the skin of a person with leprosy.
The tree is given human characteristics of feeling pain and healing.
The earth acts as an anchor holding the tree firmly in place.

rules.rule_en: The poet of 'On Killing a Tree' is Dr. Gieve Patel.
The poem was published in his 1966 collection titled 'Poems'.
The 'bleeding bark' refers to the sap that flows from the tree when it is wounded.
The main theme is the resilience of nature and the cruelty involved in destroying it.

worked_exercises.prompt_en: Can a 'simple jab of the knife' kill a tree?
worked_exercises.answer_en: No, a simple jab of the knife cannot kill a tree because it has deep roots and the ability to heal its wounds.

worked_exercises.prompt_en: What does the phrase 'leprous hide' mean?
worked_exercises.answer_en: It refers to the rough, uneven, and discolored bark of the tree, which resembles the skin of a person suffering from leprosy.
